doc.title: Bill Kirchner interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2021

title: Pitch modules technique from Brookmeyer and Albam
summary: He studied in the BMI Jazz Composers' Workshop and uses three-note pitch modules to generate melodies and harmonies, as in the Airmen chart.

bands.name: U.S. Air Force Airmen of Note

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well that anticipated a question, because you were assigned a groove so to speak. What comes next? Does the melody come next or the chord sequence or the form?

Well you know what I did? In 1989 and ’91 I spent two years studying with Bob Brookmeyer and Manny Albam in the BMI Jazz Composers’ Workshop. And they taught us a technique called “Pitch Modules” where you take three note pitch cells and use it to develop raw material from which to write music. And I teach it to all my composing/arranging students and I tell them, tongue in cheekedly, that using this

technique is much better than waiting to break-up with your significant other for an inspiration. So in this case, when I wrote this chart for the Airmen of Note, and often when I’m writing, you know, original music, I’ll use this “Pitch Module” technique just to develop raw material. And it can, from that can arise melodies or harmonies. You can use these rows of notes that come from the pitch module to derive whatever you want, in essence. So in essence what happened with that chart, the Airmen of Note, is I came up with the melody and I came up with some countermelodies and I came up with some harmonies as a result. So after you do the work you go through and just find stuff that you like and let nature take its course.
